sections.html:
Montgomery Township is the largest municipality in the North Penn area of Montgomery County, along PA 309 near the Bucks County line. It covers 10.63 square miles of land, largely built out with suburban neighborhoods, and the 2020 census counted 25,862 residents. A July 2025 estimate puts it at 26,210.

Its downtown is Montgomery Square on PA 309, and the township's ZIP code is 19454. The township also includes parts of villages shared with neighbors: Colmar and Fortuna with Hatfield Township, and Christy and Eureka with Bucks County and Horsham Township. Little Neshaminy Creek drains most of the area, which puts it in the Delaware watershed. Neighbors include Horsham, Lower Gwynedd and Upper Gwynedd townships, the borough of Lansdale and Hatfield Township, plus New Britain and Warrington townships across the line in Bucks County.

The township was incorporated on May 17, 1714. Alexander Edwards, one of the first settlers, was born in Wales and wrote "of Montgomery" in his will before his death in 1712. Many Welsh families settled in this part of old Philadelphia County, and the county that formed on September 10, 1784 was probably named for Montgomeryshire in Wales. The Knapp Farm earned a National Register listing in 1976.

The population curve explains the housing stock. The township had 850 residents in 1930 and 2,700 in 1960, then 5,718 in 1980 and 12,179 in 1990. It reached 22,025 in 2000. The count more than doubled during the 1980s, a 113 percent jump, and rose another 81 percent by 2000, so many houses here come from those two building waves.

sections.h2: How do Montgomery Township housing and income figures look?
sections.html:
Owners live in 89.4 percent of the township's homes, and median household income is $134,074. Each row is from the Census Bureau's profile of the township.

Turnover is low, with 92.0 percent of people in the same house as a year before. Foreign-born residents are 19.3 percent of the total, and Asian residents are 22.2 percent. With a typical home value near $473,000, a pricing gap of even a few percent is worth many thousands of dollars.

The average household has 2.61 people, children under 18 are 20.6 percent of the population and seniors are 20.4 percent. Owners pay a median $899 a month when no mortgage remains, against $2,408 with one, and broadband reaches 95.8 percent of households.

sections.h2: What roads and transit connect Montgomery Township?
sections.html:
Several major routes cross the township:

  • U.S. 202 runs southwest to northeast through the center on a parkway-style road.
  • PA 309 runs north to south on Bethlehem Pike through Montgomery Square.
  • PA 63 follows Welsh Road along the southwestern edge, and PA 152 passes through the eastern corner on Limekiln Pike.
  • PA 463 crosses on Cowpath Road and Horsham Road, and County Line Road marks part of the Bucks County boundary.

SEPTA runs Suburban Bus routes 94, 96 and 132 to Montgomery Mall. Workers spend an average 29.0 minutes getting to their jobs. A plant hardiness line between zones 6b and 7a follows a ridge near Stump Road, and Montgomeryville averages 29.9 degrees in January and 74.3 in July.

sections.h2: Does Montgomery Township require an inspection when a house is sold?
sections.html:
The township's fee schedule lists a Use and Occupancy permit for residential property only for new construction, at $150, with other occupancy permits aimed at manufactured homes and non-residential space. The schedule does not list a resale permit for an existing house. Call the township at (215) 393-6920 to confirm for your address, since a homeowner association or your buyer's lender can add their own steps.

Any work you did on the house is a separate question. Montgomery Township publishes residential requirements and a list of projects that need permits, so collect your permit history before listing. The Codes and Permits office is at 1001 Stump Road, with posted weekday hours of 8:30 to 4:30.

sections.h2: How do taxes, homestead and appeals work for a Montgomery Township seller?
sections.html:
Assessed values for county, municipal and school bills come from the county Board of Assessment Appeals. A yearly appeal is due August 1 ahead of the tax year at issue, and exemption applications share that date. The early date lets the board finish hearings by October 31 and notify owners and taxing districts by November 15.

A homestead exclusion trims the taxable value of a primary residence. A March 1 filing reaches school taxes starting the next July 1, and a December 15 filing reaches municipal taxes in participating municipalities starting the next January 1. The rule that concerns sellers is that a sale clears the exclusion automatically, so the seller files nothing and the buyer applies fresh. A denial may be appealed within 40 days.

The county also warns that mailed filings can be postmarked late. Ask the post office for a hand-cancelled postmark or deliver the paper to the Norristown office.

sections.h2: What is the transfer tax and what disclosures apply in Montgomery Township?
sections.html:
Transfer tax on a Montgomery Township deed runs 2 percent of the price, according to the county Recorder of Deeds. A deed claiming an exemption must carry the Department of Revenue's REV-183 Statement of Value. For deeds dated July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027, Montgomery County's common level ratio factor is 3.36.

Pennsylvania's Seller Disclosure Law has a seller complete a disclosure statement and get a signed, dated copy to the buyer ahead of the agreement. No investigation is required, but a known defect may not be left out or misdescribed. Anything that turns inaccurate before settlement must be corrected, and a buyer has two years after settlement to bring a damages claim.

sections.h2: What happens if taxes are unpaid, and what are the ways to sell?
sections.html:
Back taxes can lead to a county upset sale, held each September and December for parcels whose taxes from two years earlier are still unpaid. Parcels that fail to sell move to judicial and repository sales. A buyer at an upset sale takes on every lien, and judicial sale parcels are offered free and clear.

For a Montgomery Township house with back taxes, the usual choices are:

  • Pay the balance, then list as usual.
  • Sell to an owner-occupant and pay the taxes off at settlement.
  • Take an as-is cash offer from a buyer who handles the condition.

Get a payoff figure from the bureau first, since penalties and interest change the comparison.

faqs.q: How much transfer tax applies to a Montgomery Township sale?
faqs.a: Two percent of the price, per the county Recorder of Deeds, collected as the deed is recorded. Claiming an exemption takes a Statement of Value.

faqs.q: Does a buyer keep my homestead exclusion?
faqs.a: No. Montgomery County removes it automatically once the deed changes hands, and the new owner files a fresh application.

faqs.q: What is the last day to appeal a Montgomery County assessment?
faqs.a: August 1, one year ahead of the tax year at issue. Exemption applications share the date.

faqs.q: Is a township resale certificate needed in Montgomery Township?
faqs.a: On the township's fee schedule, the residential Use and Occupancy permit is for new construction. Call the township at (215) 393-6920 to confirm, since your buyer's lender or an association may want other paperwork.

faqs.q: What must a Pennsylvania seller tell a buyer about the house?
faqs.a: Known material defects, listed on a property disclosure statement that is signed, dated and delivered before an agreement of transfer. Subjects include the roof, basement, plumbing, heating, wiring and drainage.
